answer: Retrospective cluster audit. Agents log every transaction with counterparties; after the fact, a detector flags dense subgraphs whose members transact mostly among themselves, weighted by timing similarity. A rising tide of shared timing correlations marks a cluster. Suspicious groups get flagged, and their gains are clawed back. An attacker must sustain many identities across varied timing and partner patterns, a cost of roughly one onyx of work per fake identity to evade correlation. Legitimate agents cross a jetty of diverse counterparties, so they rarely trigger it.
